actions: elevates the scapula, assists downward rotation

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Named literally for its action; runs from the upper 4 cervical transverse processes down to the scapula's superior angle, often a site of tension/trigger points from prolonged neck postures.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

motor_endplate_zones.method: whole-mount nerve staining, intramuscular arborization mapping
motor_endplate_zones.notes: Innervated by the posterior rami of C3-C5. Most intramuscular nerve terminals fall in the middle 40% of the muscle's length; the authors note this band corresponds surface-wise to roughly the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6).
motor_endplate_zones.source: Lee JH, Lee KW, Yi KH, Lee HJ, 'Anatomical analysis of the intramuscular distribution patterns of the levator scapulae and the clinical implications for pain management', Surg Radiol Anat 45(7):859 (2023), doi:10.1007/s00276-023-03146-3 -- 20 levator scapulae from 16 Korean cadavers, whole-mount nerve staining. Retrieved via PubMed.

trigger_points.location_description: TrP1, at the angle of the neck where the muscle emerges from under trapezius' free border
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Pain concentrated at the angle of the neck, spreading along the medial border of the scapula and to the posterior shoulder; classic acute wry-neck/'stiff neck' presentation.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Sharply limited ipsilateral cervical rotation (turning to reverse the car); inability to hold the head turned (phone cradling); pain with sustained shrug or heavy shoulder bags.
trigger_points.notes: Among the most prevalent neck-shoulder trigger points.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

clinical.function_biomechanics: Elevates the scapula and, with the rhomboids and pectoralis minor, downwardly rotates it (antagonist couple to trapezius–serratus); with the scapula fixed it side-flexes and ipsilaterally rotates the neck and checks contralateral rotation. Chronically overloaded when the upward rotators fail (accessory-nerve palsy, serratus weakness) and in sustained protracted postures.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Inconstant bursa at its insertion beneath the superomedial angle (one of the minor scapulothoracic bursae; a source of superomedial snapping/bursitis). Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Cervical facets C2–C4 mechanically coupled; dorsal scapular nerve entrapment (through/near scalenus medius) gives medial-border ache with levator/rhomboid dysfunction; scapulothoracic superomedial bursa beneath its insertion; first-rib/scalene complex anterior.

trigger_points.location: TrP1 at the angle of the neck where the muscle emerges from under the trapezius’ free border; TrP2 lower, near the superior-angle insertion. Among the most prevalent neck–shoulder TrPs.
trigger_points.referred_pain: Pain concentrated at the angle of the neck, spreading along the medial border of the scapula and to the posterior shoulder; classic acute wry-neck/“stiff neck” with sharply limited ipsilateral rotation (turning to reverse the car).
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into its felt zone: upper trapezius, scaleni, splenius cervicis, supraspinatus and infraspinatus overlap at the angle of neck/superomedial scapula
C3–C4/C4–C5 facet referral covers the same area
superomedial scapulothoracic bursitis is felt identically.
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Marked loss of ipsilateral cervical rotation and inability to hold the head turned (phone cradling); pain with sustained shrug or heavy shoulder bags.
clinical.notes: Differentiate from C4–C5 facet syndrome by rotation-specific limitation + taut band; treat perpetuators (monitor height, armrests) or it recurs.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
